//: TEMPLATE — copy this file, do not edit it in place. cp appsettings.Development.template.json appsettings.Development.json (the copy is matched by .gitignore line 107, 'appsettings.Development.json', so it stays out of git), then fill in the values for your machine. Supplying the same values through environment variables works just as well and is what a deployment should do: ConnectionStrings__CatalogDbConnectionString, Migrations__ApplyOnStartup, Seed__Enabled, Swagger__Enabled, HttpsRedirection__Enabled. Note that the base appsettings.json is now free of the connection strings, so without this file (or the environment variables) the host fails on the first database call with a message that says exactly that.
//ConnectionStrings: LOCAL CREDENTIAL. These values match the 'db' service in docker-compose.yml (postgres:16-alpine published on host port 5433, POSTGRES_USER dev-only). If you changed the compose credentials, change them here too. ONE database serves both sides: the write side (DomainDbContext) writes to the `write` schema and the read side (StoredDbContext) reads from the `read` schema; the transactional outbox lives in `outbox`.
//Migrations: true is safe HERE and only here: this is a single developer's laptop or a CI job, where the convenience of 'dotnet run just works' outweighs the fact that a web process is a mediocre place to run DDL. Leave ApplyOnStartup false everywhere else and run 'dotnet Catalog.App.dll --migrate' as an explicit deployment step.
//Seed: true populates an empty database with the sample catalogue (30 foods / 25 recipes / 2 plans). DbInitializer is itself idempotent — it returns early when Foods already exist — so re-running is harmless, but this flag is what makes it opt-in rather than something that happens because the provider happened to be relational.
//Swagger: true serves the OpenAPI document at /swagger and /swagger/v1/swagger.json. It used to be implied by ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development; now it is a decision you make.
//HttpsRedirection: true ONLY because launchSettings.json publishes this app on https://localhost:63883 too, so this process really is the TLS edge for the local developer. Inside a container it must be false: TLS terminates at the ingress and plain HTTP is what arrives.
